lines.text: New Windsor. Decr 28th 1780.
D Sir,
I have the pleasure of introdu-
cing to your acquaintance the Marquis de la
Fayette a Majr Genl and as an offic. of rank in the servce of France, in the American Army, - His
Genl family, fortune & illustrious connexion in
France are alone sufficient to entitle him to our
highest respect, but when the obligation which
America is under to him aware for his
early attachment to her rights, - his great zeal
& powerful support of her cause are known
I am persuaded it will give you pleasure
to shew him every civility in your power.
It is probable that he may be accom-
panied by his Brother in law the Count de
Noailles, & Count de Damas, two gentn of fami-
ly, fortune & rank in the French Army at
Rhode Island. whose zeal to serve America lead them to make
a Southern Campaign this winter, if they
can obtain permission of the Count de Rochambeau
Commanding the French Army at Rhode Island
- Should this event take place I beg leave
to recommend them also to your attention.
With much esteem & regard
I am D Sir
Yr Most obedt Servt
G Washington

modernization.modern_text: New Windsor. Decr 28th 1780. Dear Sir, I have the pleasure of introducing to your acquaintance the Marquis de la Fayette a Major General and as an officer of rank in the service [?] of France, in the American Army, - His General family, fortune & illustrious connexion in France are alone sufficient to entitle him to our highest respect, but when the obligation which America is under to him aware for his early attachment to her rights, - his great zeal & powerful support of her cause are known I am persuaded it will give you pleasure to shew him every civility in your power. It is probable that he may be accompanied by his Brother in law the Count de Noailles, & Count de Damas, two gentlemen of family, fortune & rank in the French Army at Rhode Island. whose zeal to serve America lead them to make a Southern Campaign this winter, if they can obtain permission of the Count de Rochambeau Commanding the French Army at Rhode Island - Should this event take place I beg leave to recommend them also to your attention. With much esteem & regard I am Dear Sir Your Most obedient Servant G Washington
modernization.plain_english: New Windsor, December 28, 1780. Dear Sir, I am pleased to introduce the Marquis de la Fayette to you. He is a major general and a high-ranking officer in the French service within the American army. His aristocratic family, wealth, and famous connections in France already entitle him to our highest respect. Furthermore, America owes him a great debt because of his early dedication to our rights, his immense enthusiasm, and his strong support of our cause, so I am sure you will be glad to show him every possible courtesy. He may also be accompanied by his brother-in-law, the Count de Noailles, and the Count de Damas, who are two well-born, wealthy, and high-ranking gentlemen in the French army stationed at Rhode Island. Their eagerness to serve America might lead them to participate in a southern campaign this winter, provided they get permission from Count de Rochambeau, who commands the French army at Rhode Island. If this happens, I ask that you also look after them and pay them attention. With much esteem and regard, I am, Dear Sir, your most obedient servant, G. Washington.
modernization.summary: George Washington writes a letter of introduction on December 28, 1780, presenting the Marquis de la Fayette to an unnamed recipient. He asks that the recipient show hospitality to Lafayette and potentially his noble French companions, the Count de Noailles and the Count de Damas.

annotations.context: Written in late December 1780 from Washington's headquarters in New Windsor, New York, this letter served to introduce the Marquis de Lafayette and visiting French officers to an associate, likely in anticipation of travel south. Following the British capture of Charleston in May 1780 and the subsequent shifts in the war, the Southern theater became the primary focus of active campaigning. Lafayette, along with officers such as the Vicomte de Noailles and the Comte de Damas from Rochambeau's forces stationed at Newport, Rhode Island, sought active combat roles in the South, where Lafayette was soon deployed to counter British operations in Virginia.
annotations.why_it_matters: Letters of introduction like this highlight the critical interpersonal diplomacy that sustained the Franco-American alliance and helped secure foreign military support vital to American independence.
discussion_questions: How does Washington balance praising Lafayette's personal social rank with emphasizing his devotion to the American cause?
Why was personal networking and epistolary introduction so vital for military cooperation during the Revolutionary War?
What role did aristocratic European volunteers play in shaping the Continental Army's operations and international standing?
